Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old male whose trauma type is rape, the trigger 'Military Topics' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and memory items coherently suggest interpersonal/close-contact danger (touch, strangers, shouting, doors, vivid sensory reliving), but military-related talk implies a trauma context that is otherwise absent. This is not supported by the threat or memory content and does not fit the formulation as a plausible trigger tightly linked to the presented threat-memory pattern.

vignette:
David, an 18-year-old tax consultant, presented with a pervasive sense of dread and an inability to navigate his daily life without intense anxiety. His struggles began abruptly following a traumatic night at his firm six months prior. He had been working late, alone in the office, when an older male colleague, who had offered to help him finish up, sexually assaulted him. During the assault, the man had shouted aggressively, his voice echoing in the empty building, and at one point, a door in the hallway had slammed shut unexpectedly, making David jump, only to be pulled back into the terrifying reality of the attack. He vividly remembered the metallic taste of fear, or perhaps blood, in his mouth throughout the ordeal, a sensation that would return to haunt him.

In the aftermath, David found his world increasingly constricted. The sounds of shouting, especially an aggressive tone, became immediate and overwhelming triggers for him. A client raising their voice during a consultation now instantly made him feel an intense, visceral sense of threat, his heart racing as if the assault were happening all over again. Similarly, the sound of a door opening or slamming, whether in his office or at home, would plunge him into a state of alarm, making him react with a violent startle, his body tensing in anticipation of danger. These specific auditory triggers, along with the unsettling experience of being alone with any man, particularly in a confined space like an office, consistently brought back fragments of the traumatic event. He would be flooded with visual memories of the office that night, seeing the fluorescent lights, the desk, the silhouette of his attacker, sometimes accompanied by that distinct, metallic taste, as if the past were replaying itself in his mouth.

The constant feeling of threat, which permeated his days, profoundly influenced how his memories surfaced. If he was walking down the street and felt threatened by a stranger approaching him, even in an ordinary situation, this heightened state of alarm would often pull him into a full-blown flashback, bringing back not just the terrifying visuals but also the profound emotional intensity of the event without any clear image at all, just pure, unadulterated terror. This pervasive sense of threat also made him hyper-vigilant to his surroundings, subtly shaping what he perceived as dangerous. Because he was constantly on edge, convinced that harm could come from anywhere, his mind became primed to interpret everyday occurrences, like a sudden noise or the presence of an unfamiliar man, as new or intensified triggers for panic.

David began to avoid going to unfamiliar places, convinced he couldn't adequately assess the danger, which severely impacted his ability to carry out fieldwork for his job. His fear was that being in an unknown environment would leave him exposed, making him even more susceptible to the sudden rush of memories. And indeed, the more intensely he experienced these distressing memories, the more sensitive he became to potential triggers in his environment. A particularly vivid flashback, where he tasted the fear and saw the scene clearly, would leave him so raw that for days afterward, even the most innocuous male presence or the softest click of a door would feel like an unbearable trigger, sending him into a spiralling panic. This cycle tightened around him, making his job as a tax consultant, which often required him to be alone with clients, especially male ones, almost impossible. He'd jump if someone touched him unexpectedly, even a colleague trying to get his attention, and he'd find himself cancelling meetings or making excuses to avoid one-on-one interactions. David sought help because he could no longer bear the constant terror that felt like it was consuming him, afraid that he was losing control of his life entirely.
